newsitem.title: UK: UK funds still negative on order-driven trading.
newsitem.headline: UK funds still negative on order-driven trading.

text.p: UK fund managers still believe the order-driven share trading regime, due to be introduced this autumn, will either make no difference to liquidity and speed of execution or will make them worse, a Reuter poll showed on Tuesday.

Order-driven trading, where shares are bought automatically and sold via computer instead of being dealt by a market-maker as at present, is intended to bring London into line with bourses overseas and improve its competitiveness.

Yet the results of the survey, carried out by Tempest Consultants for Reuters, show that fund managers remain sceptical of the benefits they will derive from the innovation, just as they were when it was first proposed over a year ago.

Some 29.5 percent of fund managers questioned -- weighted to reflect the size of funds under control -- believe the liquidity of FTSE 100 stocks will suffer under the new regime, compared with 19 percent who believe it will improve.
Some 51 percent said they expect it to make no difference.
Speed of execution is expected to worsen by 53.4 percent of those questioned and to get better by only 18.2 percent.
However the findings are a slight improvement on last year's survey, when 35.7 percent expected liquidity to deteriorate and 58.7 percent expected speed of execution to worsen.
The overall cost of trading FTSE 100 stocks is also expected to improve by 61.3 percent of funds, up from 48.8 percent a year before.
"One conclusion is that there has been some warming towards the changes," said Tempest. "This said there is a consistent and deeply-felt expectation that liquidity and speed will suffer."
No-one at the London Stock Exchange (LSE) was immediately available to comment on the findings.
After a series of consultations with its members through the past year, the LSE is currently testing its order-driven system for a planned October launch.
The survey findings were part of an annual poll of fund managers giving their ratings of individual stock analysts.
